_comment: release-deny.json — the vocabulary the RELEASE gate refuses, and NOTHING else reads it.
DELIBERATELY SEPARATE FROM secrets-exclude.json. That file's patterns run through
redact() at INDEX time over the user's own memories. A brand or employer term placed
there would be scrubbed out of the author's own corpus, which is destructive and wrong:
a memory may say anything about its owner's employer. A file SHIPPED to strangers may not.
TWO TECHNIQUES, chosen for what each is actually good at:
* tokenHashesSha256 - exact known literals (brand, staff, customers, the author's
username). Sha256 so THIS FILE NEVER CONTAINS THE TERMS IT DETECTS: a deny-list
written in plaintext would itself be the leak in a public repo. Same trick
secrets-exclude.json already uses for known credentials. Regenerate with
scripts/hash-release-terms.mjs, which takes the terms on stdin and prints hashes.
* patterns - structural shapes that cannot be enumerated: private IP ranges, network
share paths, emails, phone numbers, street addresses, product model numbers.
PERSON NAMES AND STREET ADDRESSES ARE NOT RELIABLY REGEXABLE. A generic
capitalised-word-pair rule flags ordinary prose - the same over-scrub the
cred-flag-p-quoted note in secrets-exclude.json warns about ('or the guard shreds the
corpus'). So: hashed exact names for the people who matter, and the structural rules
are signals a human reads. That trade is affordable here because the target is a
~66-file code tree, not a memory corpus - a few false positives cost a minute of
review, not a shredded corpus.

danfrancislyon@gmail.com is the author's DELIBERATE public contact address, carried in the README on purpose so the project is findable. It is allowlisted here rather than exempted in code, so the gate still refuses every other address including the author's work one.

patterns.name: street-address
patterns._note: BEST EFFORT, NOT A GUARANTEE. Address shapes vary far more than this list; it missed 'Amphitheatre Parkway' before Parkway was added, and it will miss others. Treat a MISS as expected and a HIT as a prompt to look, never the reverse.
